# Question

**Do artificial sweeteners cause weight gain?** Fowler et al. (2008, *Obesity*) followed 3,682 San Antonio Heart Study participants for 7–8 years, comparing diet-soda users with non-users on BMI change and overweight/obesity incidence.

## Data source

Baseline 2×2 back-calculated from the published figures; ΔBMI SDs derived from published CIs. Observational cohort — users vs non-users were not randomized.

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Mean BMI change over 7–8 years by diet-soda consumption"
d = df[df["metric"] == "mean_dbmi_kg_m2"].sort_values("value")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
ax.barh(d["group"], d["value"], color="#4c72b0")
ax.set_xlabel("Mean ΔBMI (kg/m² over follow-up)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Methods & results

Two-proportion z and Fisher exact for the overweight/obesity contrast, odds ratio with bootstrap CI, 100k-replicate randomization; published incidence ORs and adjusted ΔBMI reported alongside.

| Analysis | Result |
|---|---|
| Overweight/obesity, user vs non-user | OR = 1.38, z = 4.44, p = 8.9e-6 · Fisher p = 1.0e-5 · rand. p = 2e-5 |
| ΔBMI over 7–8 y | users +1.48 vs non-users +1.01 kg/m² (+47%, published p < 0.0001) |
| Published incidence ORs | 1.93 (overweight), 2.03 (obesity) |

# Decision

A **strong observational association** — consistent in the cross-section and the incidence analyses. But causation is unproven: reverse causality (overweight people switching to diet soda) and confounding by baseline adiposity remain live alternatives.
